text: EXISTS doesn't care what a subquery returns — only whether it returns anything at all. That single idea gives you a cleaner way to ask "does this have a match," and its opposite, "is this missing."

Where EXISTS, select 1, from invoices, where vendor ID matches the outer supplier. SELECT 1 is a convention — the column list doesn't matter, Oracle stops the instant it finds one matching row. Every supplier with at least one invoice, same result as an INNER JOIN, phrased as a presence test.

Flip it to NOT EXISTS, and you get suppliers with zero invoices — the direct alternative to lesson eight's left outer join plus IS NULL. Same rows, read as "no matching invoice exists" instead of "joined to a NULL."

Here's why this course prefers NOT EXISTS over NOT IN. If even one row in that subquery's invoice ID column is NULL, NOT IN silently returns zero rows — not an error, a total, quiet failure. NOT EXISTS never has that problem — it only asks whether a match exists, so a stray NULL in there can't corrupt the whole comparison.

Use LEFT OUTER JOIN plus IS NULL when you also need columns from the other table for matched rows, in the same query. Use NOT EXISTS when all you need is the presence test itself — it tends to read more directly as exactly that question.
EXISTS for presence, NOT EXISTS for absence, and watch out for NOT IN's NULL trap. Next lesson: finding duplicates — a different kind of data problem entirely.
